query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys for harsh corrosive and mechanical environments, a stable, nanocrystalline passive oxide film formed through controlled microstructural refinement (via elements such as Mo and minor boron additions) governs the simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion. This refined microstructure promotes the formation of a uniform, adherent, and protective oxide layer that both limits corrosive attack by reducing ion dissolution and enhances wear resistance by lowering friction through improved load distribution.
generation.material_initial_state: A representative CoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloy with a relatively coarse-grained, untreated microstructure lacking enhanced passive film formation.
generation.intervention: Process modification through techniques such as mechanical alloying with subsequent annealing and/or microalloying (e.g., with boron) to induce grain refinement and promote in situ formation of a coherent passive oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under mechanical wear conditions (such as sliding contact) at room to moderately elevated temperatures typical of geothermal or marine environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanocrystalline grain structure and the associated lattice distortion that facilitates the formation of a thin, uniform, and adherent oxide film (possibly containing TiB2 or other composite oxide phases if dopants are used).
generation.mechanism: Microstructural refinement increases grain boundary area and enhances element homogenization, which promotes the in situ formation of a passive oxide film when exposed to oxygen. This film acts as a dual barrier: it inhibits corrosive ion transport and provides a hard, low-friction surface to resist mechanical wear. The presence of elements such as Mo further stabilizes the oxide film and improves passivation, while boron doping may induce beneficial precipitates that support grain refinement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated high-entropy alloy samples will exhibit lower wear rates (i.e., reduced material loss and lower friction coefficients) and lower corrosion current densities compared to untreated, coarser-grained baseline alloys. Moreover, the combined degradation (wear + corrosion) will be less severe than the simple sum of their individual effects, indicating a synergistic protective performance due to the passive film.
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy samples with a coarse-grained microstructure and minimal inherent passive oxide film formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions where a stable, continuous passive film can form—namely, environments that offer sufficient oxygen for oxide formation and mechanical loads that do not entirely remove or damage the film. It may fail if wear rates are so extreme that the film cannot reform or if environmental conditions (such as very high temperatures or reducing atmospheres) inhibit oxide stability.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative relationships linking grain size reduction, passive film composition/thickness, and the resultant improvements in wear and corrosion resistance remain uncertain. The optimum dopant levels and processing conditions for maximizing this synergy require further systematic investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set undergoing mechanical alloying with boron microalloying and annealing to induce nanocrystalline refinement and promote passive oxide formation, and a control set maintained in a coarse-grained, untreated state. Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under sliding wear conditions.
measurements: Surface analysis (SEM, XRD, EDS) to confirm the presence and uniformity of the passive oxide film
Wear rate (mm³/N·m) and coefficient of friction
Electrochemical corrosion parameters (corrosion potential and corrosion current density via polarization tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., lower wear rates, lower friction coefficients, and reduced corrosion current densities) relative to the untreated baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of a robust passive oxide film, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It was found that, by reducing the Mn concentration (to 5 at.% Mn), the CoCrFeMnNi alloy acquires higher yield strength values after annealing at 1117 K (from 387 to 477 MPa) due to the grain refinement effect (from 4.4 to 2.61 µm) []. Mn also shows a rapid evaporation effect during melting processes; hence, in our study, this element was replaced by Mo, which could improve the resistance to high temperatures []. Co–Cr–Mo alloy is widely used for manufacturing of vanes and gas turbines due to its excellent fatigue behavior and wear resistance [,,,]. In such alloys, molybdenum has a beneficial effect on passivation capacity, contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer that allows pitting corrosion to be limited [,]. Studies were conducted to estimate the effects on the microstructure and properties of alloys with different Mo contents [,,]. Such alloys have been designed for the manufacture of furnace casings and chemical tanks used in high-temperature and corrosion conditions [], for components used in the geothermal industry [,], or to obtain high-performance coatings [].

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

This study demonstrates that the proposed alloy design delivers substantial improvements in both wear and corrosion resistance. The work clarifies how boron doping modifies the microstructure, establishes the linkage between microstructural features and performance, and derives general design principles for engineering coatings. We define this strategy as a generalized methodology for coating performance enhancement. While the present study does not address specific service environments, machinability, or long-term stability, we contend that with its robust performance foundation, the coating can be further optimized through compositional tuning and post-processing to enable reliable service across a broad range of applications.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
